parts.note: read not as the psychological linking of thoughts but as a body of clever people pooling their ideas, a panel of experts

explanation.surface: A psychology term for how one thought calls up another.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase looks like the textbook term for mental connections; the question mark tells you to read 'association' as a group of people and 'ideas' as what they supply.
explanation.definitionFit: A panel of experts who answer questions or advise is an association whose stock-in-trade is ideas.

parts.note: refers to the old music-hall song Daisy Bell, whose singer admits the marriage won't be stylish but offers a two-seater machine for the couple

explanation.surface: Someone called Daisy is getting married in a rather unstylish carriage.
explanation.walkthrough: The song Daisy Bell ("Daisy, Daisy, give me your answer do") says "It won't be a stylish marriage" and promises a seat on one built for two: hence 'inelegant union'.
explanation.definitionFit: The song's suitor offers a two-seater pedal machine, the transport for an unstylish wedding.

indicators.note: odd here means strange or peculiar, telling us the letters of the word pair are rearranged

explanation.surface: An unusual couple departed and were gone for four weeks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd' tempts you to take alternate letters, but it is the anagram signal: PAIR rearranged gives APRI, then L for left.
explanation.definitionFit: The fourth month of the calendar, between March and May.

clue.text: Keep fresh first in the city

indicators.note: first says the word for fresh goes at the front, before the word for keep

parts.note: fresh means new
a keep is the fortified tower of a castle, so castle stands for it

explanation.surface: An instruction to keep something fresh before anything else in town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep' reads as a verb, but it is the noun: a castle's stronghold. 'first' puts NEW ahead of CASTLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A major city in north-east England on the River Tyne.

parts.note: split legends into leg ends; the little piggies are the digits in the nursery rhyme This Little Piggy, counted on a child's foot

explanation.surface: Asking about the folk tales told of small pigs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Legends' is to be read as LEG-ENDS, what sits at the bottom of a leg; 'say' flags the wordplay on the word. The nursery rhyme 'This little piggy went to market' is counted on a child's foot.
explanation.definitionFit: The digits at the end of the foot are what the nursery rhyme counts off as piggies.

parts.note: high life is read not as glamorous society living but as life lived on raised ground, in the hills

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a man leads a glamorous society existence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High life' suggests luxury and glamour; the question mark says take it literally, life on high ground, which belongs to a hill dweller.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone from hilly country lives a life that is literally high up.

indicators.note: changing tells us the letters of worth are to be altered into a new order

explanation.surface: An actor line-up whose value keeps shifting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changing' rearranges WORTH.
explanation.definitionFit: To cast and to throw both mean to fling or toss something.

clue.text: Head of chemistry in wrong university department

indicators.note: in says one piece is placed inside the word for wrong

parts.note: wrong means faulty, defective

indicators.note: Head of means take just the first letter of chemistry

explanation.surface: The chemistry chief has been placed in the wrong section of the university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of chemistry' looks like a job title but gives C, which goes 'in' FAULTY.
explanation.definitionFit: A faculty is a division of a university grouping related subjects, such as science or arts.

parts.note: U is the film classification abbreviation for universal

indicators.note: mystery signals that the letters of Red Barn are puzzled over and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written; the Red Barn Murder was a notorious 1827 English crime

explanation.surface: Recalls the Red Barn Murder, a famous English killing of 1827, as a universal mystery.
explanation.walkthrough: The Red Barn Murder (1827, Polstead, Suffolk) was a famous case, so 'mystery' reads as part of the story; it signals the anagram of RED BARN, giving NBARRED after U.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unbarred has had its bars drawn back, so it is open.

clue.text: Where talc is scattered for acrobatic feat

indicators.note: is scattered means the letters of where talc are spread about into a new order

explanation.surface: A gymnast dusts talc on the floor before a tumbling move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is scattered' rearranges the nine letters of WHERE TALC.
explanation.definitionFit: A sideways handspring with arms and legs spread like spokes, a gymnastic move.

clue.text: Compete with Olympic finalists, like some old characters

parts.note: to run in a race is to compete

indicators.note: finalists here means the final letters of the word Olympic

explanation.surface: Competing in the Olympics alongside athletes who reached the final.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finalists' looks like sporting talk but means the last letters of OLYMPIC, IC, after RUN.
explanation.definitionFit: Runes are the letters of ancient Germanic alphabets, so old writing characters can be described this way.

clue.text: Monastic room — a right place for wine-store?

parts.note: a monk's small private room is a cell

explanation.surface: A monk's tiny room might be just the place to keep wine.
explanation.walkthrough: CELL plus A plus R; the question mark admits that a wine store is only one use of an underground room.
explanation.definitionFit: An underground storeroom is the traditional place to keep wine.

parts.note: military jargon for a rocket fired skyward, read instead as something scooped from the ground and hurled into the air

explanation.surface: A military rocket fired from the ground at aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: The military term is to be read literally: a ball packed from what lies on the ground and thrown upward.
explanation.definitionFit: A packed ball of winter flakes is gathered off the ground and thrown through the air at someone.

clue.text: Played out iron returned to bazaar

indicators.note: returned means the symbol for iron is turned round and read backwards

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
a bazaar is a fete, a fundraising fair

explanation.surface: Worn-out iron goods brought back to a charity sale.
explanation.walkthrough: FE 'returned' gives EF, then FETE.
explanation.definitionFit: Effete means exhausted, having lost its vigour, i.e. worn out.

parts.note: a minor, cut-down form of French is its abbreviation Fr
a battle is an action in military language

explanation.surface: A small skirmish forming part of a French war.
explanation.walkthrough: 'minor' looks like it describes the battle, but it shrinks French to FR.
explanation.definitionFit: A fraction is a part or portion of a whole.

clue.text: For men, no place initially in cordial surroundings

definitions.text: For men, no place initially in cordial surroundings

indicators.note: surroundings says the word for cordial encloses the other letters

parts.note: cordial means warm and friendly, hearty

indicators.note: initially means take the first letters of no and place

explanation.surface: Somewhere warm and welcoming where men are not allowed.
explanation.walkthrough: N and P, the first letters of 'no place', go inside HEARTY; the whole clue also describes a pre-wedding celebration where men have no place.
explanation.definitionFit: A bride-to-be's celebration with her women friends is a festive gathering men are barred from.

clue.text: Male topic, perhaps, concerned with a classification of heavenly bodies

definitions.text: concerned with a classification of heavenly bodies

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters of male topic might be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: A masculine subject of discussion, maybe about astronomy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges the nine letters of MALE TOPIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Ptolemy's ancient system arranged sun, moon and planets around a fixed Earth, a scheme ordering celestial bodies.

clue.text: Column of soldiers in Mount Tumbledown?

indicators.note: in places the word for soldiers inside the rearranged letters
Tumbledown, a Falklands War battle site, here says the letters of Mount tumble into a new order

parts.note: soldiers are men, as in officers and men

explanation.surface: A line of troops on Mount Tumbledown, a hill fought over in the 1982 Falklands War.
explanation.walkthrough: Mount Tumbledown is a real battlefield, so 'Column of soldiers' reads as a marching file; 'Tumbledown' scrambles MOUNT and MEN goes 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: A column such as Nelson's is a memorial pillar, a commemorative structure.

clue.text: Third party insurance for girl walking out?

definitions.text: Third party insurance for girl walking out?

parts.words: Third party insurance for girl walking out?
parts.note: motor-insurance jargon read literally: an extra person who goes along to protect a young woman on a date

explanation.surface: Asking about car insurance cover for a young woman driving off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Third party insurance' is car-cover jargon; 'walking out' is the old phrase for courting, so the third party is a chaperone keeping the girl safe.
explanation.definitionFit: An older companion accompanied a young woman on outings with a suitor to ensure propriety.

parts.note: to crow is to gloat or boast
a bar is a counter where drinks are served

explanation.surface: A burglar boasting at the pub counter about his tool.
explanation.walkthrough: A jemmy (US jimmy) is a burglar's short crowbar.
explanation.definitionFit: A jemmy is a short prising bar used by burglars to force doors and windows.

parts.note: jumbo suggests a large passenger jet, but here it is an elephant and the shaded seat is the canopied carriage on its back

explanation.surface: A window seat with the blind down on a jumbo jet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jumbo' suggests a jumbo jet; it is an elephant, Jumbo being a famous one.
explanation.definitionFit: The canopied seat strapped onto an elephant's back for riders in India.

indicators.note: out signals the letters of dishing are put out of their order

explanation.surface: Handing out thrashings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges DISHING.
explanation.definitionFit: A thrashing or a heavy defeat, both being a beating.

parts.note: a lower is something that lows or moos, such as an ox
a tongue is a language

explanation.surface: Coarser speech used in the interval of a boxing match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lower' is not 'more low' but one who lows; 'between rounds' is a sandwich filling, between rounds of bread.
explanation.definitionFit: Cooked cattle tongue is a classic cold meat to put between slices of bread.

indicators.note: Extract from says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A passage taken from a long, amusing tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'yarn' suggests a story; it is the thread.
explanation.definitionFit: A synthetic fibre spun into thread for textiles.

parts.note: self-raising suggests baking flour, but refers to the Shakespearean idiom of the engineer hoist with his own bomb

explanation.surface: A risky kitchen gadget, like flour that rises on its own.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet's 'hoist with his own petard': the bomb that lifts the man who set it.
explanation.definitionFit: A small bomb for blasting gates, famous for blowing up its own engineer.

clue.text: Stage direction of Harlequins, for example

definitions.meaning: an instruction in a script for a line spoken to the audience unheard by others on stage
Harlequins is a London rugby union club, so it is one team

explanation.surface: A theatre instruction found in a Harlequin pantomime.
explanation.walkthrough: Harlequin suggests the pantomime figure, but Harlequins is a London rugby club, so 'a side'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both an actor's remark to the audience and a sports team, read as one team.

definitions.meaning: the ... flows through Durham in north-east England
to brook is to tolerate or put up with, as in to stand for it

explanation.surface: A river or a stream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brook' looks like a stream to match 'River', but it is the verb meaning tolerate.
explanation.definitionFit: A Durham waterway, and informally to accept or put up with something.

parts.note: BR is short for British Rail
oil is a grease or lubricant

explanation.surface: A cooking method involving lubricant from a railway.
explanation.walkthrough: British Rail was the UK's nationalised railway, abbreviated BR.
explanation.definitionFit: To grill food under direct heat, the US term for grilling.

definitions.meaning: raising someone to a higher rank
an architect's drawing of one face of a building

explanation.surface: Moving up the ladder for an architect's achievement.
explanation.definitionFit: Raising to higher rank, and a scale drawing of a building's facade.

clue.text: They are held to attack Brazil

definitions.text: They are held to attack Brazil

parts.words: They are held to attack Brazil
parts.note: Brazil seems the football nation, but it is the large hard-shelled nut, gripped and crushed by a hand tool

explanation.surface: Players are being restrained to stop them going after the Brazilian team.
explanation.walkthrough: Brazil is the country; read it as a brazil nut, which these hand-held crushers attack.
explanation.definitionFit: A hinged hand tool for cracking the shells of hard fruits like walnuts.
